sub_criteria.name: extraction accuracy
sub_criteria.text: Measures LLM claim-extraction accuracy from full papers or abstracts against expert/human annotation, ideally broken down by paper section, claim type, or model.

sub_criteria.name: evidence-link errors
sub_criteria.text: Characterizes how claim-to-evidence links (passage, table, or citation) fail: fabricated support, wrong-direction reads of contradicting evidence, or over-generalisation past the paper's conditions.

sub_criteria.name: benchmark construction
sub_criteria.text: Describes how a claim-evidence or citation-grounding benchmark (e.g. SciFact, CiteME, or similar) was built, and what its reported numbers can or cannot legitimately support.

sub_criteria.name: abstention and calibration
sub_criteria.text: Tests whether abstention or calibrated uncertainty improves the trustworthiness of extracted claims, and reports the coverage cost of doing so.

sub_criteria.name: cross-model or cross-domain generalisation
sub_criteria.text: Reports whether extraction or grounding results replicate across different models, domains, or paper types, or whether they are inflated by benchmark artifacts.

items.abstract_600: Chart understanding plays a pivotal role when applying Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to real-world tasks such as analyzing scientific papers or financial reports. However, existing datasets often focus on oversimplified and homogeneous charts with template-based questions, leading to an over-optimistic measure of progress. items.abstract_600: Evaluating aligned large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize and reject unsafe user requests is crucial for safe, policy-compliant deployments. items.abstract_600: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) presents challenges, particularly for retrieval models within these systems. Furthermore, evaluation of the retrieval model's performance based on query-document relevance labels shows a small correlation with the RAG system's downstream performance. items.abstract_600: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has recently emerged as a method to extend beyond the pre-trained knowledge of Large Language Models by augmenting the original prompt with relevant passages or documents retrieved by an Information Retrieval (IR) system. items.title: Synthesizing scientific literature with retrieval-augmented language models
items.abstract_600: Scientific progress depends on the ability of researchers to synthesize the growing body of literature. Can large language models (LLMs) assist scientists in this task? Here we introduce OpenScholar, a specialized retrieval-augmented language model (LM)1 that answers scientific queries by identifying relevant passages from 45 million open-access papers and synthesizing citation-backed responses. items.title: MMLongBench-Doc: Benchmarking Long-context Document Understanding with Visualizations
items.abstract_600: Understanding documents with rich layouts and multi-modal components is a long-standing and practical task. Recent Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have made remarkable strides in various tasks, particularly in single-page document understanding (DU). However, their abilities on long-context DU remain an open problem. This work presents MMLongBench-Doc, a long-context, multi-modal benchmark comprising 1,062 expert-annotated questions. items.abstract_600: The automation of scientific discovery has been a long-standing goal within the research community, driven by the potential to accelerate knowledge creation. items.title: An automated framework for assessing how well LLMs cite relevant medical references
items.abstract_600: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to address health-related queries, it is crucial that they support their conclusions with credible references. While models can cite sources, the extent to which these support claims remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce SourceCheckup, an automated agent-based pipeline that evaluates the relevance and supportiveness of sources in LLM responses. items.title: Personalization of Large Language Models: A Survey
items.abstract_600: Personalization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has recently become increasingly important with a wide range of applications. Despite the importance and recent progress, most existing works on personalized LLMs have focused either entirely on (a) personalized text generation or (b) leveraging LLMs for personalization-related downstream applications, such as recommendation systems. items.abstract_600: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has recently become a very popular task for Large Language Models (LLMs). items.abstract_600: Document visual question answering (DocVQA) pipelines that answer questions from documents have broad applications. items.title: The Art of Saying No: Contextual Noncompliance in Language Models
items.abstract_600: Chat-based language models are designed to be helpful, yet they should not comply with every user request. While most existing work primarily focuses on refusal of"unsafe"queries, we posit that the scope of noncompliance should be broadened. We introduce a comprehensive taxonomy of contextual noncompliance describing when and how models should not comply with user requests. items.abstract_600: We present a principled approach to provide LLM-based evaluation with a rigorous guarantee of human agreement. items.abstract_600: This survey examines evaluation methods for large language model (LLM)-based agents in multi-turn conversational settings. items.title: LitLLM: A Toolkit for Scientific Literature Review
items.abstract_600: Conducting literature reviews for scientific papers is essential for understanding research, its limitations, and building on existing work.
